utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If the witness could be brought in. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours, I wanted to update Your Honours regarding the scheduling for the rest of the week or the remainder of the week. Mr. -- we spoke to Mr. Brakovic yesterday at the end of the afternoon, and he will be available to testify tomorrow afternoon. I believe we're sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. He did inform us that he can't stay in The Hague beyond Friday evening because he needs to attend to some personal family matters back home, so he request if we could try to complete his evidence by Friday. I think we sit in the morning on Friday, so by the end of our hearing on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We do sit in the morning on Friday. We have no present way of knowing whether we can meet his wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to follow-up on scheduling, after we complete the testimony of Mr. Brakovic, we will continue with witnesses as they had been scheduled, that is starting with Ms. Hajrizi and continuing on to Mr. Latifi and the other witnesses that had been listed in our notification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence is cooperative and prepared to complete the testimony of those witnesses by Friday, but we do have a concern. On several occasions so far, the Prosecution has informed the Tribunal that a witness can only testify for one day or half a day here because of some urgent personal or professional matters, thereby allotting in advance the time for this witness's examination. On several occasions, it turned out that this was not correct. Let me just bring up the case of Mr. Brakovic. In the notice we received last week, the Prosecution insisted that his testimony must be completed by the 4th or the 5th because he could not remain in The Hague. And now we see that he can remain here for the 5th and the 6th and the 7th of May. The same went for Witness Dunjic and some other witnesses. I don't want to make a mistake, so I'm not going to be mentioning their names. Now we received a notice for two witnesses, one expert, one -- an ordinary witness, although he's also an expert because he's a forensic scientist, indicating that their testimony must be completed by a certain date. I think this is exerting pressure on the Trial Chamber and the Defence in terms of the length and scope of the testimony of those witnesses, and the Defence is prepared to do its best and will do its best to have the two witnesses complete their evidence by the end of this week and so that they could go back to their duties, but we don't think that this practice on the part of the Prosecution is proper. The witnesses should be brought here at the time when they are able to remain at our disposal for as long as necessary, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide how long that is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we're appreciative of the sense with which you and Mr. Djordjevic have been seeking to cooperate with the efficient completion of the trial and accommodating the personal needs of witnesses. We're grateful for that, and we will certainly keep our eye on the matter that you have just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. If I could remind you the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Ms. Kravetz is continuing with her questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, when we broke off yesterday we were speaking about your research mission to Kosovo in July 1999, and you explained to the Chamber your findings based on your investigations there in the municipality of Djakovica. During this research mission in July 1999, did you visit any other municipalities in Kosovo province?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I was in Pristina municipality. That's where I was for the most part based and located during that period. I would have also visited the Srbica and Glogovac municipalities, and I spent extensive time in the Pec municipality. There are probably others that I'm not recalling, but those were the primary locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during the time you expended in Pec municipality, did you visit Pec town?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to interview residents of Pec town during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on the accounts you heard during these interviews, what did these persons, these residents, of Pec town tell you about what had happened in the town during the period of the NATO bombing, I mean following the start of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most consistent story in Pec was about forced expulsions. The residents told me how security forces rounded them up, forced them from their homes, and ordered them to leave the city in a very organised manner, in some cases involving buses organised by the local authorities in which people were loaded onto and transported out to Montenegro. In some cases, families had more specific stories of killings. I can recall two in particular that they believed involved the same group of perpetrators, and then they also spoke about more large-scale killings in the neighbouring villages, which was something I then pursued.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before we move to what you've been referring to about the killings, the accounts you heard of killings, could you tell us how long or for how many days you were in Pec conducting these interviews.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could check my notes to give you a precise number and dates, but for sure I spent at least five days in the area, if not a week, because one of the nearby villages became the -- a focus of our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us a little bit about the methodology that you used in your interviews with residents of Pec when you were conducting your investigations there. Were they similar to the type of interviews you spoke about yesterday that you carried out in Djakovica, or were they different in any way?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methodology for our interviews is uniform across Kosovo and in every other place where we work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were these interviews conducted in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. There were some individuals who spoke English, but the vast majority were conducted in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you yourself speak Albanian, or were you assisted by an interpreter during the conduct of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak Albanian, although most of the interviews I was assisted by an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, during the days that you spent in Pec town, were you able to observe any damage or destruction to civilian property?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify that previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To say "assisted," I mean the interviews were conducted in English with the interpreter, and I was not the one -- I mean, I would use my Albanian to introduce myself and general informalities, but the crux of the interviews were conducted with the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the days that you spent in Pec town, were you able to observe any damage or destruction to civilian property?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were any neighbourhoods of Pec town particularly affected by this damage, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such detail, I'm afraid I don't. I definitely recall extensive destruction in central areas of Pec, so not in the peripheral zones, but in what might be called down-town Pec, although Pec is not large enough to say it really has a down-town, including destruction by what appeared to be a fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And did any of the persons that you interviewed, the residents of Pec town that you interviewed, were they able to provide any information as to how this damage to civilian property had been caused and by whom?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The information from Pec was consistent and in my view reliable because people were in the town and in the -- in Pec city up until late stages of the war, some -- not everyone from the town had been expelled. And so they testified that these structures had been set alight by the state security forces, either police -- I don't recall now whether Yugoslav Army forces they said were present in the town itself, but certainly police and what they referred to as local militias.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you see any destruction to any mosques in the town of Pec?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall seeing at least one mosque, but my memory on that is not precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you told us that you heard accounts of killings that had occurred in Pec town in neighbouring villages and that one specific incident became the focus of your work. Could you tell us a bit more about that, which incident you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: During our investigations -- my investigation in Pec, we heard stories about what people called a mass killing, or in their words it was a massacre, in a nearby village called Cuska or in Albanian Qyshk. It's 5 or 6 kilometres approximately to the east of the city, and the reports were consistent enough and credible enough to merit us taking a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to speak with any eye-witnesses or -- who had information about how this massacre had taken place?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a considerable amount of time, at least four, probably five days on this trip and returned again on numerous occasions. I could give you the precise times exactly how long I was there by checking, but I spoke with a large number, I would estimate approximately 20 different people, who had -- were from the village or two surrounding villages. It was Cuska, Zahac, and Pavlan. These three villages might be considered in one general operation. It was the same day in which the alleged crimes took place and spoke extensively with people who were witnesses to these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did they tell you had happened in the village of Cuska, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall very well, and I subsequently published an entire book, co-authored an entire book just on the Cuska killings. In Cuska was one of the unique cases in the Kosovo conflict not because of the sheer numbers. In Cuska, 41 men were killed; in Zahac, 19; and in Pavlan, 6, all of them on May 14th, 1999. Those numbers in and of themselves are not unique. There were many other places in Kosovo in which such a large number of people were killed, but the evidence here was very striking and on a level that I as a human rights investigator had rarely encountered before. Specifically, the villagers told me that security forces that had entered the village on May 14th in the morning sent a lot of the women and children away after taking their goods, their personal property, their money; and then there were some killings around different areas of the village. But there were groups -- a group of 29 men were separated and taken into three private homes. And in each of those homes, security forces lined them up and opened fire, killing the men in these homes, and then lighting the homes on fire. And what was unique to me from their testimony is in each of these cases there was a survivor. One man in each of the homes somehow managed with very minimal injuries to survive this mass killing. And so, of course, we tracked down -- I tracked down these people, and they were able to give me incredible -- incredibly dramatic testimony, eye-witness testimony, which we had received in some other cases in Kosovo but it was rare. I mentioned Bela Crkva yesterday in which we also had a surviving witness, but these gentlemen were able to give incredible details that matched what we had heard from the other witnesses. And the other -- the third factor that raised this to a new level for me as an investigator was that the villagers, including these men who survived, claimed to have recognised the perpetrators and have known them personally. And furthermore, we obtained photographs of what was told to me were local militia members and police members from the Pec area. I obtained these separately from Cuska village. The villagers had no idea they existed. They didn't give them to me. I obtained them in Pec, and I scanned them on to my laptop and showed them not just to the villagers in Cuska but to people in general, saying, I've obtained these photographs, do you know who are these people? And to my surprise, the villagers in Cuska and to an extent in Zahac and Pavlan recognised these men. And I undertook incredible efforts because I realised the potential of leading a witness to not make any suggestions about who these individuals were. I showed them on my laptop. I always -- I took people one on one and just opened the picture on the laptop and said, Do you know who this is? Without suggesting that this was someone from the Pec area or any other sort of leading insinuation. And we had multiple, multiple positive IDs, and we had extensive discussions with our lawyers in-house about what we could say publicly, and we decided we could only release a name if we had at least three individuals who separately said they had identified this individual in the same way, not just, I know him, or I -- but that is X person or Y person, and those names are mentioned in the reports -- in the book and in the report that we subsequently published.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is the name of this report that you published regarding your investigation on the Cuska killings?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report that Human Rights Watch published is called "A Village Destroyed," and we subsequently released it as a book together with photographs and text co-authored by myself and a photographer named Gilles Peress and another writer named Eric Stover. It was a separate production published by the University of California Press.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, this Human Rights Watch report, "A Village Destroyed," do you recall when it was published, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The research was in July. It continued afterwards. It would have been the latter stages of 1999 if my recollection serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we spoke a little bit about the practice of Human Rights Watch regarding dissemination of reports. Would this report have been sent to Yugoslav and Serbian authorities in the same way as other reports that you spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the dissemination procedure would have been the same. Just to add one brief point on the Cuska case which made it even stronger, there were media investigations, also, into this case, and they were able to locate some of the perpetrators and interview them. And we cite those interviews in the report, although I didn't conduct them myself, but it adds to the holistic picture of what took place in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that during these investigations you discovered that approximately 40 men had been killed or 41 men in this village. Based on the accounts of survivors and eye-witnesses, did -- were these persons who were killed in this village involved or engaged in fighting in any way?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villagers and the witnesses uniformly testified that there had been no KLA presence in the village, that there had been no fighting in the village, and those statements were not thrown out there on face value. They were part of comprehensive interviews that extended for many, many days and involved excruciating detail. I should add also that I of course visited the sites, the homes where the men were killed, spent extensive time in the village, and the physical evidence that I observed was also consistent with their stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you had told us that you had obtained photographs of persons that were later identified as perpetrators. Just to be clear, these photographs, are they also contained in the Human Rights Watch report that was published, "A Village Destroyed"?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this report into evidence. This is 65 ter 00397.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00755, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Abrahams, to move on to another report. In your different statements, you speak extensively about a Human Rights Watch report "Under Orders." Could you very briefly explain your involvement in producing this report.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would categorise my involvement as the coordinator of the project, but it was a collaboration among the Human Rights Watch staff. We -- we -- it involves various sections, which include the background of the conflict from 1990 to 1998; the period of what we consider to be the armed conflict, 1998 and 1999; and then the period after which was also a very important focus for us, what happened after June 12th and particularly revenge attacks against Serbs and Roma and non-Albanians in Kosovo. My role was to coordinate and manage the researchers who were on the ground during the NATO bombing. I also went there myself to conduct research in Albania and in Macedonia. Of course, then myself and other researchers entered Kosovo in June and July and afterwards in later 1999, so then I was responsible for compiling and organising all of this material.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you personally draft any of the sections of the report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have spoken about your investigations in Djakovica and also in Pec municipality. Is the information that you obtained during these research missions in those municipalities contained within this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would these -- the sections that refer to Djakovica municipality and to Pec municipality, would these have been sections drafted by yourself or by other colleagues?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted both of the sections you mention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when the report "Under Orders" was made public by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And again, I presume that this report, following the normal procedure of Human Rights Watch, was disseminated according to standard practice and to Yugoslav and Serbian authorities and to other persons on the human rights mailing list that you spoke about yesterday. Would that be a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In addition with "Under Orders," we translated the entire report into both Serbian and Albanian languages. We held press conferences in Pristina and in Belgrade, and I participated in both of those. The Belgrade press conference had representatives of the government on a public panel we had as well. So the coverage in this report was -- was extensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have prepared excerpts - I spoke about this yesterday - of this report which are the sections on Djakovica and Pec, and these have been uploaded in the e-court system as 65 ter 004380.1. I know my learned colleague has raised an objection to the report in itself, but at this stage I would seek to tender these -- this exhibit, the extracted portions, and ask that it would be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Consistently with our position, they should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00756 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I want to ask you about another report which is referred to in your July 2006 statement and also in your previous statement of January 2002, and this is a report entitled "Rape As a Weapon of Ethnic Cleansing." Could you please explain what was your involvement in the preparation of that report.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That report was researched primarily by my colleague, a woman. We felt that was necessary in order to gain the confidence and interview female victims of sexual assault. I was her advisor, a guide, and I also was heavily involved in helping her draft report and edit the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you participate in any of the interviews that are contained within this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted some of the interviews with medical professionals and others with second-hand knowledge -- or in some cases direct knowledge of sexual violence, but not the victims themselves, again, for the trust factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you go about trying to obtain information on cases of rape or sexual assault that had taken place during the 1999 conflict?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of rape first came to our attention during the period of NATO bombing in April. I was in northern Albania with my colleague Joanne Mariner, and in the refugee camps we became aware of a reported or alleged cases of rape of I believe three women. I don't remember at this moment - I could check - how we became aware of it. I believe it was from a doctor in one of the refugee camps who had -- who had alerted us. I'm not certain about that. I can't testify exactly how we learned of this case, but we ended up -- my colleague Joanne ended up interviewing these women who testified about the sexual violence they had experienced, and we ended up issuing a statement based on that testimony during that time, in April. Then when we all entered Kosovo in -- after June 12th, then Joanne and another colleague who did the bulk of this work, Martina Vandenberg, she went around and she identified the victims through multiple ways but by speaking with local women's organisations that were dealing with rape survivors, by speaking with gynaecologists and other doctors who were treating rape survivors, and there may have been other -- other leads that I'm not aware of at this -- I'd have to refer to the report to give you further examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, was the methodology that you and your colleagues used in preparing this report similar to the methodology that was used in the other reports that you have been speaking about during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the process -- the interview process, how that was conducted, both with the victims and with the -- the interviews that you conducted yourself with persons who could provide evidence or information on rape and sexual assault.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, it's the same one-on-one setting, but in cases of rape and sexual assault there's additional importance to the confidentiality and trustful rapport that an interviewer establishes with an interviewee or an alleged victim. In particular in the Albanian society - I think in any society but particularly in the Albanian society - it is an extremely shameful experience to have suffered from rape or sexual assault. It is a taboo subject in the Albanian culture, would make women very difficult to find a husband if they wanted to marry. And so making sure we could interview these women in a proper way would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness has again gone beyond the limits of fact testimony, and now he is presenting his conclusions, and as a fact witness he should not be testifying in this manner, and now we have gone into the sphere of morality and ethics of an ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we need to make any specific ruling or observation on that at the moment given our general position. Carry on, Ms. Kravetz, but be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When was the research for this report concluded, if you recall? I mean, for how long were you -- your team -- was your team working on this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The field research was approximately three weeks. I believe the precise dates are presented in the report, and then the writing and editing process would have gone on a number of weeks after that, usually longer, probably I would say two months after the end of the field mission. So I believe this report was published in the end of 1999, maybe early 2000 if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, I presume when it was disseminated according to the usual procedure of Human Rights Watch and sent to all competent authorities that were on your mailing list, both Serbian and Yugoslav authorities --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this report is Exhibit 00386. I know an objection has been raised with regards to its admissibility, so I seek to tender it at this stage and ask that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00757, MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 00388 up on the screen, and I ask that only the English be displayed for the witness so he can read the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, do you recognise the document that is up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain what this is.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statement about rape that I referred to previously. During the period of the NATO bombing, we produced what we called the Kosovo Human Rights Flashes. These were in essence short reports or press statements issued during the fighting about various incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had spoken yesterday about the information you had obtained when you were in northern Albania regarding an incident that occurred in Meja. Would that information have been contained in one of these Kosovo Human Rights Flashes at the time? Was this the type of information that you would include in this type of report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were these type of Human Rights Flashes only issued by Human Rights Watch during the period of the conflict, that is, during the period of the 1999 conflict from March to June 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We issued regular press releases or press statements prior to and after the NATO bombing. During the NATO bombing, given the intense attention, understandably, to the region we produced what we called the flashes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were these Human Rights Flashes disseminated? To whom were they sent?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were disseminated in the same manner as all of our other material, although not by post. They wouldn't have been mailed. There were many of them. They put by e-mail, and I'm not sure if also by fax. I would have to check if they were sent by fax, but definitely by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how would you go about -- when you received information from eye-witnesses or survivors, how would you go about trying to corroborate that information?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the corroboration was based on the interviews we were conducting in the refugee camps in Albania and Macedonia, and we held ourselves to a very high standard. I mean, just looking at this report, I can see we had two direct victims as well as eight other women in the village who gave corroborative elements of their stories. So that's a good example of the standard we set for ourselves when making serious allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, before making public allegations of this sort you would try to obtain corroboration. You wouldn't only rely on the account of one person but you would try to investigate and research the allegations before going public with them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not just try. It was a requirement as dictated by our mandate and responsibility to achieve a high standard of corroboration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that this Human Rights Flash report here has two dates. On the top, it says updated February 22nd, 2000, and then there's also a second date below, April 28th, 1999. Would the core allegations of rape that are contained here have already been contained in the Human Rights Flash that was issued in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I do not know what precisely was updated on February 22, but the core allegations of rape and sexual assault were made on April 28th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So when you -- if I understand correctly, when you would issue such a report, for example, you were speaking about the Meja incident earlier. If you obtained additional information with regard to a certain incident, would you then issue an updated Human Rights Flash report on that same incident?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually not, unless there was some additional information of substantive value. In this case, I don't know what exactly was updated, but it is a sign of our transparency because if there was any change to the web site, then -- which would have been the update. This would have been updated on the web site. Then we wanted the readers to be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. This is 65 ter 00388.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During the period that you were investigating or conducting your investigations for the report "Under Orders," did you investigate violations committed by all sides of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and not only for "Under Orders," but from the beginning of our involvement and our investigations in Kosovo we strove stridently to investigate all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Does the -- does part of the order "Under Orders" contained, also, references to violations committed by -- or against Serbians and other minorities in Kosovo, or is it only focused on the Kosovo Albanian community?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the beginning, we looked at violations by the Kosovo Liberation Army, issued a series of statements, chapters in reports, and later reports about violations by the KLA. Those are contained and elaborated on in "Under Orders," and in addition, we also looked at the behaviour and alleged violations by NATO and repeatedly criticised NATO's use of cluster munitions during its air war in Yugoslavia and civilian deaths caused by NATO during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have very few questions left. I wanted to ask you some questions about a section of your statement, the January 2002 statement. In your statement, you discuss extensively the background to the Kosovo conflict, and you speak about events that occurred in the early 1990s and even before then. Could you tell us what is the basis for the information that you have provided in your statement regarding these events.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two essential sources: Academic and individual, if I can call it that. Most of the history is what is available in the public domain, through recognised and accepted academic literature as well as journalistic; and then from my personal conversations and understandings, having worked in the Balkan region since 1993, having studied east European history, and thereby having accumulated a knowledge of these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic, you cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, and I am a member of the Defence team for the accused, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic. I have Marie O'Leary, a member of my team, with me here. I will have some questions for you and will ask you to provide us with some explanations if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up Exhibit P758, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, this is flash number 31, updated in February of 2000. Am I right if I say that you cannot tell us which part of the document was in fact updated in 2000?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be able to check that information for you, but at present I cannot, no. The date is February 22, 2000 sorry I got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. I have a question for you which relates both to this document and some other documents. According to this flash, at least, you had a doctor in Albania examining the victims; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct that we had a doctor, but we spoke with a doctor who had treated this -- these victims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I see that you identify yourself with Human Rights Watch, but what I wanted to say, of course, is that there was a doctor in Albania who examined some victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you as an investigator ask the doctor to provide you with the medical documentation that was the result of the examination of the victims?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall if we did or did not. That's a question I can ask my colleague Joanne Mariner who conducted the research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at any point in time take possession of any medical documentation relating to any of the victims?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reference to this statement on sexual violence or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, first off in relation to sexual violence.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check the report to answer your question precisely, but in some of the cases I believe the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Right. You're saying that without checking up on that. In view of your work, did you hand over the evidence concerning rape to the investigators of the ICTY, to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement, Flash 31, and our subsequent reports were made available to the ICTY investigators. Whether we specifically informed them of any particular victims is something I do not recall. It is possible that we did, but I'm not certain if that took place or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I'm quite surprised to hear this answer of yours. Please answer my questions, and my question had to do with medical documentation and not any other sort of evidence. Did you at some point hand over some medical documentation concerning rape to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me personally, I did not, but I do not know for sure whether my colleague Joanne or Martina Vandenberg did or did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Not only her, I believe that there was also Mrs. Anderson who prepared the report on rape, but let's move on. Since this is the third time you're testifying before the ICTY in The Hague, have you ever been shown medical findings concerning the rape of any of the victims you interviewed in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not interview any rape victims or victims of sexual assault.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the interpretation was wrong. Mr. Abrahams, can you please read the transcript. This is the third time you're testifying before the ICTY in The Hague. Have you ever been shown medical findings of any of the victims of rape you or your organisation interviewed? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reading it to be sure I'm understanding you exactly. Me personally, I'm not aware -- I don't believe I was ever given medical records about rape victims. That's something that would have been provided to my colleagues who conducted the research, which were Joanne Mariner and Martina Vandenberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I will put the question again. During the trial against Milosevic or the trial against Milutinovic where you appeared as a witness, as you do today, were you ever shown medical documentation concerning rape victims that were interviewed by your organisation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the trials, no, I don't recall being shown that sort of documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you shown any sort of medical documentation yesterday or today which has to do with victims of rape that your organisation interviewed or any other sort of medical documentation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Abrahams, you told us yesterday that you were a trained researcher of Human Rights Watch. Can you tell us what exactly your training consisted of.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All researchers in the organisation go through an extensive training in-house on how to conduct investigations, how to interview witnesses and victims, collect supportive or evidentiary material and secondary sources; and that formed the crux of my training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us that you started -- or interviews with victims and witnesses started to be taped as with the onset of the era of digitalisation. Can you tell us whether back in 1998 and 1999 this sort of method was applied in Macedonia, Albania, and in Kosovo in general.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, no, it was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were written statements given by victims and witnesses signed by them at all?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not HRW, Human Rights Watch, procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you've already explained that to a certain extent, can you tell us whether in 19 -- or rather, in 1998 who was it who interpreted or did the translation of the interviews you had in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our interpreters were individuals from Kosovo, most of whom were at that time working as journalists and have subsequently gone on to careers as professional journalists in international media, such as AP, Agence France Presse and other agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnicity of the interpreters before they started working as journalists?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what period and investigation we're discussing. The journalists I'm referencing here were ethnic Albanians. We also had two Serbs -- Serbian citizens and ethnic Serbs on our staff at different periods, and some of the research was conducted by them -- I'm sorry, I strike that, by one of them. One of them stayed in Belgrade, but one of them was working in Kosovo, and this person obviously speaks Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained to us the extent of your knowledge of the Albanian language. Let me ask you about the other researchers, now, Fred Abrahams, Bogdan Ivanisevic, Andre Lommen, Joanne Mariner, Martina Vandenberg, Benjamin Ward, James Ron. Do they speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How can you be sure of the accuracy of the interpretation done by the ethnic Albanian interpreter taking a statement of the ethnic Albanian witness or victim? How can you be sure that the interpretation was correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two ways. The first is these interpreters were people with whom we had worked for a long time and had established a high level of trust. The second is these interpreters also worked with us when we were investigating crimes by the Kosovo Liberation Army, often at some risk to themselves. Obviously, the KLA did not want to be investigated. And our interpreters undertook those risks, translated honestly, and further earned our trust through their willingness to also examine the ethnic Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have come to the right spot that I want to discuss. How could you be sure that they were not members of the Democratic Alliance of Kosovo or of the KLA but in mufti? How could you be sure that they were not members of some other organisation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- the interpreters, you're asking about? These individuals to the best of my knowledge had no political affiliation, and my knowledge was extensive because Kosovo is small; I had been travelling there and working there since 1995; and individuals, activities, and political views are known. But furthermore, their political affiliations were secondary to their professional behaviour, and whatever group or party they may or may not have belonged to, the importance for me and my colleagues was that they translated, interpreted honestly and accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot resist putting the following question to you. All the statements that were given to you which you claim were credible, didn't they seem strange to you for the fact that they followed the same pattern, and repetitions do lead to suspicions, don't they?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not seem strange to me. They had details and specifics about what they had seen or experienced that were credible. I say "they." I mean, we -- for "Under Orders," we interviewed more than 600 people, so I can -- I don't want to paint them all with one stroke. But the repetition you refer to, if it existed, I took to mean -- I interpreted as the widespread nature of the crimes they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you rule out the possibility that all these individuals were groomed about what they were supposed to say and how they were supposed to say it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- let me rephrase that. Certainly, there was an interest on the part of the Kosovo Liberation Army to hide some of its activities and to portray the crimes of the Serbian forces in a certain light. There's no doubt about that; there was a motivation. And all forces to the conflict were interested to control information. That's why our interview process was so important, why we take extra care, especially in times of armed conflict, to conduct lengthy and professional interviews. The cases that we reported through -- in "Under Orders" and in other documents met that standard of corroboration in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The victims and witnesses you interviewed, did they have an opportunity to read the statement once you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they asked to review it, we would allow that, but usually they didn't, and so that that rarely came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to me now what was the technique you used in taking statements in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We recorded them by hand primarily and sometimes recorded. I mentioned before digital recording, but of course cassettes were available and were occasionally used as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In what language were the statements formulated?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, statements formulated, you mean the questions asked? I'm sorry, what do you mean by "statements formulated"? Recorded? If you mean recorded, then English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you said that in 1998 and 1999 you wrote the statements by hand, and my question was: In what language were the written statements recorded? And if you need to repeat your answer now that you're certain of the question, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were recorded in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told -- talked extensively about the sending of reports over the past two days. Yesterday, you told us that in the course of 1998 and through to the end of June 1999 you were also sending reports to the KLA. Do you have proof of you sending reports to the KLA in this period from the start of 19 -- or, rather, from 1998 through to the end of June 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Distributing the reports to the KLA at that time were -- was difficult because they had no official presence or diplomatic representation, but the statements were distributed to the Albanian media -- Albanian-language media, both in Kosovo and in Albania and Macedonia. I was also handing them out when possible when I visited in Kosovo, and there was -- at times there was a KLA representation in Pristina. For a brief period in 1998, they had a sort of media office, or a political representation is perhaps a better way to describe it. And I did meet with those people and gave them copies of our material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of material was it, and who did you hand it over to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office at that time was run by a man named Adem Demaqi, and he would have been the recipient of some of this material. I do not recall exactly what I gave him, but it's fair to assume that the report "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo" would have been something that he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday that from 1996 onwards, the reports sent to the official dignitaries in Serbia were sent by organisation to their e-mail addresses. Was my understanding correct or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They were sent to the e-mail addresses that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, I claim upon full responsibility that from 1996 through to the end of war in 1999, the MUP of Serbia did not have a web site of its own at all where it could have published its e-mail address or through which it could have communicated with third parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- that is not really a question. That is a statement made by my learned colleague. I would ask that he put a question to the witness and avoid making statements on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it does need some rephrasing, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where did you get the information from to the effect that the MUP of the Republic of Serbia had an e-mail address in 1996, 1997, 1998, and 1999, and could you tell me what the e-mail address was?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP did have a web site, but I do not know when exactly it went on line. I can certainly check that information. The MUP e-mail was to the best of my knowledge on our list, but I have to check that list to be sure that's true. This list is in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, when you're talking about the e-mail addresses and the web site, which year are you exactly referring to? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly when the MUP web site went on line. That can be checked. As for the e-mail address list, it was created by 1996 and constantly updated since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You yourself did not engage in these technical details or businesses?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not manage the list, but when I obtained an address that I thought should be added to the list, I provided it to our technical -- my technical colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I wanted to say or to ask you was that you were not the one sending the e-mails to these various state institutions and governmental agencies; is that right? That's what I meant by you not doing the technical part of the job.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided the material - for example, a statement - and the technical colleagues would push the button, if you will, send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you receive any evidence of the receipt of your reports to the addressees? You yourself, did you receive any such proof?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The e-mail addresses that rejected our mail were then deleted from the lists. So in that sense, I was aware of which addresses were not functioning or not receiving the material we had sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. We'll get back to that, but let me now ask you: Am I right when I say that all those notices that you were sending to the officials in Serbia and Yugoslavia were also submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal and that yesterday they were admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall if the material was formally submitted, and certainly not at that time, not in 1996; by 1998, I'm not sure. But it was -- in other words, I'm not sure that we officially presented it, but it was in the public domain, and certainly it was obtained -- and I was aware that it had been obtained by the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P742 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, this is the front page of this document. Could you please tell me whether there is a cover sheet to this fax? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in your report, do you perhaps have the fax cover sheet for the letter that was sent to Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic on 20th of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in the report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at this letter. Do you notify Mr. Stojiljkovic about any of the crimes in this letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter of inquiry requesting information from Minister Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Human Rights Watch have any proof to the effect that any of the reports that you drafted and sent to him from 1998 until the end of June 1999 were actually received by Mr. Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received any reply from Minister Stojiljkovic, so I do not know whether he received this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the Milosevic trial and the Milutinovic trial and over the past two days here, were you shown any proof that Mr. Stojiljkovic actually received any of your reports drafted in the course of 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that the address on this letter is the well-known address of the Ministry of the Interior, 103 Knez Milosa Street, 11000 Belgrade, Yugoslavia, and that there is no e-mail address of the Serbian MUP listed here?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter was sent by fax, a fax which was -- which went through. It was confirmed that it went through, and I don't believe it was sent by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, is there a fax number of the Serbian MUP here? Is it noted here?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is there the fax number from which this fax was actually sent?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the section of the letter that I can see on my screen, no, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down to the end of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So now you can see the whole of the letter.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I see here, no. Perhaps there was something on the top of the page, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, now you can see the top of the page too.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These faxes were sent through a computer server, which would describe why -- which would explain why there's no number on the page that we are seeing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that you don't have any proof that this letter was actually sent in the manner that you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could consult with my colleagues in New York who might have computer evidence that it was sent, but on my person and here now, no, I don't have that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we please have Exhibit P743 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, could you please tell me who -- or, rather, this facsimile cover sheet, who was it sent to with the attachment?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you as an expert, don't you think that this is a very general term, if I told you that I sent something to the US Army, for instance?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be more precise, this was sent to the information service of the Kosovo command of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To the information service. And what command are we talking about? What kind of a military unit was it, the one that you sent this document to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the office -- the communications office or the media office of the Yugoslav army that was dealing with Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, now you say here the Kosovo command. What unit do you mean when you say "Kosovo command"? What is it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my memory, it was the 3rd Army that was in charge for southern Serbia and Kosovo. There was also a Pristina Corps that was responsible for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what information service was this sent to, in what town or city?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, how was this letter sent in technical terms?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you remind me of the date in which this letter was sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 20th of July - we'll see that later - 1998. It's a whole series of letters that all bear the same date, but we looked at those two letters yesterday. Let's speed things up a little bit, Mr. Abrahams. Do you see an e-mail address anywhere, an e-mail address of this body that you sent this document to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see the fax number, or rather, the telephone number or ...

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 of this document, and then I'll conclude with this document, and then we'll have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, could you please read the addressee of this letter.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojska Jugoslavije, Kneza Milosa 33, 11000 Belgrade, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. Well, one of the questions was whether you were able to speak or understand the Serbian language. That was one of the questions that I wanted to ask you, and now I got my answer. Do we have a fax number or an e-mail address anywhere here?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From what I see on my screen, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that this is an address in Belgrade that has nothing to do with the information service command of either the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree. The Yugoslav Army was headquartered in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you. They were headquartered in Belgrade. That's what you read, but information service of the 3rd Army or of the Pristina Corps was not located in Kneza Milosa Street in Belgrade. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they were located or what communication they had with -- between Pristina and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, could you please tell me, whom did you send this letter to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to the information service of the -- what we called here the Kosovo command, but I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time for our technical break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, we stopped at this letter of yours sent on the 20th of July, 1998. Am I right - if you look at the contents of this letter - that you do not bring up any crimes perpetrated by the Yugoslav or Serbian forces against anyone in this letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter informs the army that we are conducting an investigation and we are soliciting their contributions or information in the process of information collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In one of the items or bullet points, you say: "Can you provide us with any military reports about the actions of the army in Kosovo since January 1998?" Am I right if I say that you did not expect to obtain any such reports because no army in the world would have given you any such reports if you had sought them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my job and responsibility to ask questions and their job to reply or not reply. We gave them an opportunity to present us with information, which they declined -- an opportunity that they declined to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do we have any proof that you sought and obtained this kind of information from NATO, for instance, or from the KLA in this period, 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Letters of this sort I do not have. And regarding NATO, my colleagues were the researchers for the investigation into NATO behaviour and compliance, NATO's compliance with international humanitarian law during the air campaign. So I would have to ask them what communications they had with NATO. Regarding the KLA, official letters to the best of my knowledge were not delivered, but there were some communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the reports that you drafted, regardless of whether you were a researcher or not, is there this proof, is it contained there, about going to NATO, looking for any kind of information, and the feedback in terms of you getting this information from them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Letters to NATO I do not have in my possession. I'm not aware of them being sent, but my colleagues would have been responsible for that -- were responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter document 00534.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, am I right if I say that this is a letter that on the 12th of July, 1996, you sent to minister of the interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Jokanovic, indicating your wish to discuss with him the recent terrorist violence against policemen, the status of human rights, and the ministry's perspectives on the future of the region?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I submitted this letter to Minister Jokanovic as well as other offices in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00097, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at 65 ter document 00533.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, am I right if I say that this letter dated the 12th of July was sent by you to Mr. Mirovic, asking him to set up a meeting with Mr. Zoran Sokolovic, Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia; the Minister for Human Rights, Mrs. Margit Savovic; the Minister of the Interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Vukasin Jokanovic; and the Commissioner for Refugees, Mrs. Bratislava Morina; and you wanted to talk to them about the recent terrorist violence, the status of human rights, the problems of Serb refugees, and the government's perspectives on the future of the region?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I should note there's a line in this letter that I currently regret or language that we subsequently changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Mr. Abrahams, when did you go to Gornje Obrinje, or, rather, when you went there on the 29th of September, 1998, was the village in the hands of the Serbian forces or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian forces had left the area of Obrinje and Drenica by, if I'm not mistaken, the 27th, if not the 26th. I would have to check to be sure of the exact day. So by the time we entered the village, they were no longer present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have document or exhibit P750. 750. It's been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you wanting the last letter exhibited, Mr. Djurdjic, the one to Mr. Mirovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document with 65 ter 00533 would be assigned D00098, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, can you please tell us, what do we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the body of one of the Delijaj family members who were killed in Gornje Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you what is it you see on the photograph. Am I right if I say that you see a body lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a full body and the head and shoulder of a second body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. You have told us that those bodies were in a dried-up river-bed. What can lead us to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conclusion is based on my personal observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I'm not wrong, you told us that in this river-bed there were seven bodies; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's a question of translation, but I wouldn't categorise it as a river-bed but more a gully. But in terms of numbers, there were seven bodies to the best of my recollection. The number for sure is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. It's possible that it was a gully or a river-bed. I'm relying on translation now, but that's immaterial. As a researcher, as a trained researcher of the Human Rights Watch, why didn't you take a photograph where we could see all seven bodies?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are photographs of the other bodies, and many of them are in the report. There are photographs that also did not get printed in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, my question to you was: As a trained researcher, you want to have your research have a high probative value. You list seven bodies that were found in the gully, yet we don't have a photograph of the scene of the crime where we could see all seven bodies in a single photograph. I'm not asking you about photographs of individual bodies because usually what you need to do is you need to have a picture or a photograph of the whole of the scene, and then you go and photograph details.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to check our video archive to tell you exactly what we photographed, but I do recall that the area was somewhat large. The crime scene, if you can call it that - I do call it that - from the first victim to the last was at least 30 metres in distance, and the gully itself was at least 10 metres long in a wooded area. So photographing the whole crime scene would have been difficult. Nevertheless, we may have done it. I would have to check our records to tell you whether that's the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you will agree with me that yesterday and today we did not see any such photographs that would show the scene of the crime as a whole?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs that showed the scene of the crime as a whole, no, we have not seen today or yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, it seems to me that a professional photographer of the "New York Times" was present with you. I -- his name escapes me now, but I'm sure that we have it in the papers; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Wade Goddard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P751 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, could you please tell me, what do we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a child from the Delijaj family who we saw and photographed -- my colleague Peter Bouckaert photographed in the forest outside of Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day we arrived and saw the bodies, I believe that was 29th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 27th of September -- 29th, okay. Yes, it's okay if it's the 29th. Yes, it's been corrected. Do you see any injuries to this body?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this photograph, I cannot -- I cannot answer that. I don't see photographs in this -- I don't see injuries in this photograph, and I don't recall -- would have to check my notes to see whether this individual had wounds. Given the fact that they were no longer alive, there was definitely some injury, but I do not recall what precisely it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abrahams, again, we don't see a long shot of the scene; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a focused shot on one body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question, but thank you. If my memory serves me right - at least, correct me if I'm wrong - you told us that in Gornje Obrinje you had seen some bodies that had been mutilated; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did we see yesterday or today any photographs of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know at this point - I have to check the report - which bodies precisely were mutilated and which ones we photographed. That information is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, please answer my questions to speed things up. My question was quite specific. Yesterday and today, did we see any photographs of any mutilated bodies here at this trial?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Maybe?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll go through all the photographs, then. Is there any mutilation on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't see it from this image, but it's possible there was. I have to check my report. I don't recall the injuries on each of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I don't know if this -- there's a mistake in the interpretation or if you're just trying to evade my answer, but judging from the transcript my questions have been interpreted correctly. Yesterday and today, in the photographs that we saw that were shown to you by the Prosecution, did we see any photographs of mutilated bodies? So it's quite -- it's a specific question. I saw or I did not see, and we're talking about Gornje Obrinje, so photographs from Gornje Obrinje that we saw here.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the bodies in these photographs may have been mutilated. I don't know. The -- the injuries of mutilation are not visible to me from these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P752, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What can we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
